note_tweet.text:
Solar and wind power have grown quickly in Poland, but coal still dominates.

The share of electricity produced by solar and wind in Poland more than doubled in just four years. In 2021, these renewable sources produced just 11% of its power; by 2025, this had risen to 25%.

You can see this growth in the chart, based on electricity data from Ember.

Solar and wind output, combined, grew very little in 2025, due to weak wind conditions. Solar output continued to grow, but it was barely enough to offset the decline in wind power.

Poland still has one of the most coal-intensive electricity mixes in Europe, with coal producing 50% of its power. The country has committed to moving away from it in the next few decades; growth in solar and wind generation will play a key role in this.

(written by @_HannahRitchie and @parriagadap)

note_tweet.text:
Tohoku University and Toyota-supplier Aisin built a 16 nm AI chip (SoC) with 32 MB of embedded STT-MRAM that holds both a compact Linux boot image and Tiny YOLOv3 (object detection AI model) weights on-chip.

No external DRAM or SSD is needed for startup or inference. It boots in 65.7 milliseconds (39× faster) and runs object detection at ~50.7 mJ/frame with big energy savings. They used weight sharing and hybrid 8/16-bit math to fit the model. 

The chip also includes on-chip SRAM (used for feature maps and other working data) and a DDR interface, so external memory can still be attached when larger models or more capacity are needed. TSMC manufactures the chip.

Nice real-silicon demo of near-memory computing for edge AI — useful for automotive cameras, sensor fusion, and always-ready devices that need instant-on and low standby power. Not revolutionary: Others – Hailo, Ambarella, Renesas, etc. – already use large on-chip SRAM, embedded MRAM, or in-package DRAM, but it’s a good example of the gains when OS + model live in non-volatile on-chip memory. $TSM $AMBA #Hailo #Renesas #semiconductors

note_tweet.text:
Zombie cells may have a kill switch

As we age, some cells stop dividing but refuse to die. 

They're called “zombie” (senescent) cells. They pile up and inflame the tissue around them which is bad for you body. 

This research group figured out how to kill them in mice. 

They found that these zombie cells run low on one fatty acid: DGLA. So they added it back causing many of the 
zombie cells to die while the healthy cells survived. 

They died by ferroptosis where the cell’s outer membrane oxidizes and breaks.

Would be interesting if replicated in humans.

Which vaccines do children around the world receive?

Every year, the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF estimate what share of children in each country get each routine vaccine. Their Estimates of National Immunization Coverage cover vaccines against 13 diseases, from measles to rotavirus, in 195 countries since 1980.

They start from the doses that health services report and check them against household surveys. For the small share of countries that haven’t reported any data for the most recent year, WHO and UNICEF estimate coverage from the years before.

The chart shown here is about the vaccine against human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes nearly all cervical cancers. It shows the share of girls who had their last dose between the ages of 9 and 14, measured when they turn 15. Coverage varies a lot from country to country, even within the same world region.

We recently updated our charts with the July 2026 release, which adds 2025 estimates for every country. For HPV, we now have data for 160 countries and territories in 2025, compared with 146 a year earlier.

(This data update was led by Tuna Acisu.)

For almost two decades, the environmental movement has repeatedly announced the demise of fossil fuels. The headlines have been dramatic, but the results have been less convincing.

As @turkiyecop31 is about to begin, the world remains remarkably indifferent — despite the climate crisis growing ever more urgent —  as if saving the planet were merely an optional item on the agenda.
@gerardreid14  and I invite @CampanaleMark , founder of @CarbonBubble. Carbon Tracker is the financial think tank that brought the concepts of unburnable carbon and the carbon bubble into mainstream debate. Its research has helped investors understand the risks of fossil-fuel investments but has also been politically weaponised by the Greens.

A decade ago, the debate centred on stranded assets, carbon budgets and the prospect that fossil-fuel reserves would become economically unviable. Today, our thinking is increasingly aligned with perspectives associated with @ember_energy and @MLiebreich, emphasising technology, economics and the practical realities of the energy transition.

We probably are witnessing a schism between former allies: the “Climate Movement” and “The Clean Energy community”. We believe technology, innovation and economics will do more to accelerate the transition than verbose toothless international accords or poorly designed top-down government policies.

Carbon Tracker deserves credit for making climate risk a serious financial issue. However, forecasts about the timing of peak fossil-fuel demand have proved less reliable. Oil demand rebounded after COVID-19, while geopolitical instability and energy-security concerns have demonstrated the resilience of hydrocarbons.

The question is whether the carbon-focused approach remains relevant or whether it is approaching obsolescence.

Environmental campaigners have advocated carbon taxes for decades, arguing that polluters should pay for emissions and that revenues should fund the transition to cleaner energy. But what if the world already has a de facto carbon tax, imposed not by environmental policy but by geopolitical conflicts? Wars, supply disruptions and decisions by powerful governments can drive up the price of oil and gas, imposing enormous costs on households and businesses. 
Russia under Putin, Iran under the Ayatollahs and the United States under Trump illustrate how geopolitical decisions can reshape global energy markets.

Carbon Tracker helped establish stranded-asset risk as a serious capital-markets concern. Its central warning—that some fossil-fuel investments could lose value as the energy system evolves—remains relevant.

But the timing of the transition has proved difficult to predict. Fossil-fuel demand has shown greater resilience than some forecasts anticipated, while geopolitics, affordability and energy security have complicated the path towards decarbonisation.

The distinction is important: identifying investments at risk is not the same as predicting the imminent collapse of fossil-fuel demand.

Our conversation was robust, with both sides standing their ground. We left with a sense that the debate needs to move beyond political targets and increasingly outdated assumptions towards the realities of technology, economics and capital allocation.

We may agree on the destination, but the real argument is about the pathway.
